title: Deep-learning resurgence from programmable GPUs and ImageNet to AlexNet-scale empirical break
pressure: Neural-network methods had long existed, but large visual-recognition problems were constrained by training compute, data scale, optimization practice and benchmark/evaluation infrastructure.
preExistingWorldModel: GPUs were highly parallel graphics processors; neural networks and backpropagation were established; labeled vision datasets and competitions were growing but large deep models were expensive to train.
candidateRoutes: hand-engineered visual features with conventional classifiers
scale labeled data and model size together
observationsAndInstruments: NVIDIA introduced CUDA in 2006 to expose GPU parallel throughput to general computational workloads.

The 2012 AlexNet work trained a deep convolutional network on 1.3 million ImageNet images and reported substantially lower error than previous state of the art, explicitly using an efficient GPU implementation.
Contemporaneous work also explored distributed training at still larger scales, indicating that compute/data infrastructure was becoming part of the research object.
decisiveTests: held-out ImageNet classification error against strong prior methods
whether GPUs make the deep model trainable within practical time
whether larger models/data continue to improve rather than merely fit the training signal
technicalOrScientificTransition: A previously known model family became newly competitive when compute programmability, labeled data, optimization tricks and benchmark evaluation crossed a joint threshold.
rivalsAndFailures: The result did not show that any larger neural network or any GPU workload would generalize.
Benchmark improvement depended on a specific data/evaluation substrate and later required out-of-distribution and broader task testing.
diffusionAndScaling: The empirical break accelerated adoption of deep representation learning across vision and then other domains.
standardsAndInstitutions: Hardware vendors, dataset maintainers, conference communities and independent laboratories supplied different pieces of the evaluation/compute ecosystem.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Compute and benchmark scale can concentrate access and create proxy incentives; benchmark success remains distinct from broad semantic performance.
secondOrderEffects: Programmable accelerators and large datasets changed which model classes were experimentally affordable, feeding a new scale-driven research regime.
sourceNativeSummary: The 2012 deep-learning break was co-produced by an algorithmic family, programmable accelerator, large labeled benchmark and practical training implementation; none alone is a sufficient history.
